prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms opened timekeeping at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep a single-part prize for B012 with Katori and Ye, and the exchange in round 1 has made my reasons more specific rather than different. What I would reward is an architecture: a lattice light field tuned so that the two clock levels shift together, which removes Doppler and recoil effects while thousands of atoms are probed at once. That is the physics that distinguishes this step from the 2005 prize, which supplied the frequency ruler, and from the 2012 prize, which supplied control of a single ion. The many-atom scheme brings its own physics, namely collisions, lattice-light and blackbody shifts, and collective effects, and these have been tracked down and are understood quantitatively. The 1e-18 comparisons between independent laboratories and the gravitational redshift resolved over a millimetre are measurements that anyone can check, and they are the evidence that the architecture works as the theory says. Ye's group owns most of that performance record, Katori owns the proposal and early strontium work, and a two-name prize states this division honestly. I do not rest this on the six-to-two count after round 1. I rest it on the fact that the attribution questions raised against this candidate are narrower than those raised against every alternative that was proposed.
statement.case_against: The reservation I take most seriously is the one Kroll and Danielsson put plainly: this rewards a measurement capability before the discoveries it is meant to enable, such as varying constants, dark matter or geodesy, have been delivered. The 2005 and 2012 prizes also leave a reader entitled to ask whether the committee is favouring precision metrology again. I think the citation must answer that by naming the neutral-atom lattice and the many-atom interrogation, and I would not defend a wording that sounds like clocks in general, since ion clocks reach comparable accuracy and their community would reasonably feel overlooked. The credit also remains open at the edges: Lemonde and the SYRTE group, the Hg lattice proposal, Takamoto, Ludlow and Hinkley are not in the pair, and I am relying on memory for the 2001 to 2005 record. As a theoretical atomic physicist I am close to this field and probably find its virtues more persuasive than a colleague from outside would.

responses.point: Olsson argues that the 1e-18 uncertainties and the millimetre redshift are Ye's results and speak to the realisation half of the citation, whereas Katori's claim rests on the 2001 to 2003 proposal and the first strontium demonstrations, so the citation should state that distinction.
responses.response: I agree, and I would carry it into the text. The performance records are not evidence for Katori's priority, and the proposal and the first demonstrations are not evidence for Ye's accuracy. My draft citation uses 'invention and realisation' to make this split visible, and the committee motivation can say who did what. I would stop short of putting names against clauses in the citation itself, because the prize is for the lattice clock as a whole and the two halves are inseparable in practice: the accuracy result would not exist without the magic-wavelength scheme, and the scheme would have remained a proposal without the systematics work. Your point about Tokyo is, to my mind, handled by disclosure, since you report no collaboration with Katori.

responses.point: Mehlig says the citation must state what is new, the neutral-atom lattice with magic-wavelength cancellation and its many-body systematics, so that it does not read as general precision metrology, and that the 2001 to 2005 priority record should be checked before the citation is fixed.
responses.response: Your wording test is the right one and I have tried to meet it: the citation names the lattice, the magic-wavelength trapping and the many neutral atoms, which are exactly what the comb and single-ion prizes do not contain. On priority I am as dependent on memory as you are, so I will not claim more than I know. My recollection is that Katori's proposal and the first strontium work are the clear origin, that Lemonde's group and the Hg proposals were close parallel efforts, and that the JILA group made the systematics decisive. If the secretariat's record shows Lemonde's contribution to the magic-wavelength concept to be on the same footing as Katori's, I would want to reconsider the names. Without such evidence I see no reason to widen the pair, and the three-person limit gives room for it. A small correction to the record: B012 was my first place at the opening, so I did not move up to it in round 1, and my stance is unchanged.

responses.point: Kroll supports B012 but discloses time in John Hall's laboratory during his PhD, with Hall being Ye's doctoral advisor, and notes that his first place is a specialist's choice. He also says Lindroth's second choice, atom interferometry, has not delivered its headline goals in the way lattice clocks have.
responses.response: I treat your disclosure as a lineage note rather than a conflict. You report no joint work or financial interest with either candidate, and the committee is entitled to know and record it. I would only ask that it be minuted so that the final ballot is understood. Your point on atom interferometry is fair, and it is the main reason B003 stays an alternative in my file and not a second part. The equivalence-principle and gravitational-wave goals are not yet reached, Chu's earlier prize complicates the credit, and a trio with Mlynek is hard to defend. You are also right that the clock has delivered its headline accuracy and redshift measurements, which is the best answer to Danielsson's tool-versus-discovery worry.

responses.point: Johansson lists the possible redefinition of the second as a timing question, says B012 is distinct as a magic-wavelength neutral-atom lattice with many-atom interrogation, and agrees that pairing it with B010 would exceed three people.
responses.response: I have thought again about timing and I side with Mehlig and Pearce on this: the committee should judge the demonstrated science, and the redefinition of the second is a decision by a standards body that the physics does not depend on. In round 1 I left timing open and I now close it, with the reservation that I would want the motivation to avoid implying that the redefinition is the reason for the prize. On B010, I agree with your arithmetic and your science. Wineland's 2012 prize and the 2022 entanglement prize narrow the ground for Cirac, Zoller and Blatt, so I keep B010 only as an alternative. A two-part prize would force one of the two names out of B012 or leave the second part with a single person, and I do not see a combination that serves either part.

responses.point: Eriksson holds B036 as the preferred configuration, arguing that the flat-band prediction and the observed correlated and superconducting phases are stable and reproduced even though the pairing mechanism is not understood, and that waiting would not add much confidence.
responses.response: I take your argument that the prize need not rest on the pairing mechanism, and I find the prediction followed by an unexpected observation exactly the kind of result I like. You have also said you would find B012 the safer choice and would accept it. My difficulty remains one of credit and verification. I cannot judge disorder and reproducibility in moire samples myself, and I would need the experimental record around Cao, Fatemi, Dean and Young to be established before naming a trio, which round 1 did not do. For that reason I do not move to B036 this year, and I would be glad to see it again when the interpretation and the credit are clearer.

uncertainties: The 2001 to 2005 priority record for magic-wavelength trapping and the first strontium lattice clocks among Katori, Lemonde, Ye and others, which I know only from memory and which could change the credited names if it showed shared origin.

Whether the wording of the citation is sufficiently narrow around the neutral-atom lattice so that the ion-clock and ultrastable-laser communities are not read out, and whether the committee accepts the distinction from the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
Whether a measurement-technology prize, with the headline payoffs in fundamental physics still prospective, is regarded as close enough to a discovery of nature by the rest of the committee.

My judgement of B036 and B057 depends on colleagues' views on maturity and credit, and my judgement of B029 on whether three names can represent a very large collaboration, so I cannot test those cases independently.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. My profile shows no collaboration with Hidetoshi Katori or Jun Ye, or with the lattice-clock community, and none with the other shortlisted names. I have worked for many years with Anne L'Huillier, a 2023 laureate, but that concerns attosecond physics and not any shortlisted ballot. I work in the same broad atomic physics field as B012, B003 and B010, and I disclose that closeness. I note Kroll's lineage through John Hall's laboratory and Olsson's Tokyo fellowship as recorded by them, and I see no reason on the information available to treat either as requiring recusal.
